  • Coree↗Historical community geography in a federal park account
    Connection & source
    Historical community geography in a federal park account

    The Coree discussion identifies Carteret and Craven counties in coastal North Carolina and explicitly locates Coree communities near Cape Lookout at European contact. This establishes a historical North Carolina connection. Inspection: Actual HTML And Who Were the Coree? paragraphs, lines 24–29, inspected. Limits: The source explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about language and cultural classification. Archaeological site attribution, disappearance assertions and equivalence with Tuscarora, Machapunga or Neusiok are not adopted. No burial information or site coordinates are reproduced.

    European-contact period and the early eighteenth century. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗
  • Eno↗Historical river community geography in state and specialist accounts
    Connection & source
    Historical river community geography in state and specialist accounts

    The state plan identifies Eno people living along the Eno River at early European contact. Jean B. Anderson's Library of North Carolina account independently locates the historical Eno in North Carolina's Piedmont. This supports a historical North Carolina connection without assigning a modern Eno government or adopting uncertain descendant-identification claims.

    Early European-contact history; state management plan dated September 2017. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗ · Supporting source 1 ↗
  • Hatteras↗Historical people name and coastal geography in specialist reference
    Connection & source
    Historical people name and coastal geography in specialist reference

    Evans explicitly identifies Croatoan/Croatan as a group later known as Hatteras Indians and locates their historical communities on North Carolina's Outer Banks. The proposed connection concerns that historical people-name usage, without deciding the present representation or recognition of communities using Roanoke-Hatteras or related names. Inspection limit: indexed original-source text was inspected; the direct page could not be rendered in this review. This is an inspected excerpt, not a full-work content check.

    Sixteenth- through eighteenth-century historical naming; essay published 2006. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗

  • Pamlico↗Historical community geography in a state hosted nomination draft
    Connection & source
    Historical community geography in a state hosted nomination draft

    The draft identifies the area that became Aurora as formerly inhabited by Pamlico, also termed Pomouik, Native Americans. Its location section explicitly identifies Aurora in Beaufort County, North Carolina. This supports a historical North Carolina route. Inspection: Actual state-hosted 72-page PDF: location field on PDF p.1; Section 8, Page 41 / PDF p.41 historical paragraph and Wetmore attribution; Section 11 preparer/date credit on PDF p.70. No complete nomination review is implied. Limits: The document is marked DRAFT; no National Register listing/approval status is inferred. The geographic paragraph is a later synthesis citing Wetmore 2006, not a new archaeological identification or an independently read original colonial record. Statements about destruction, enslavement or absorption following war are not adopted as proof of disappearance or current identity.

    Indigenous habitation before the later town of Aurora; early colonial historical context. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗

These are starting lists, not a complete census. Modern borders help you navigate; they are not Indigenous homeland boundaries. A connection may be historical or present-day and does not imply presence throughout a region. Directory names can overlap; the profiles explain their relationships.
